ABOUT THIS EDITION

This is a full Bible in the Shona language of Zimbabwe. The "IBS" in the abbreviation likely refers to the International Bible Society (now Biblica), which has been involved in producing Shona Scripture translations. Shona is a Bantu language spoken by approximately 10 million people, primarily in Zimbabwe. Bible translation into Shona has a long history, with the Bible Society of Zimbabwe publishing the first complete Shona Bible (the Mongenster translation) in 1949. Multiple Shona Bible editions have been produced over the decades, including the 1949 version revised in 2002, a Trinitarian Bible Society New Testament in 2014, and the Shona Contemporary Bible published by Biblica in 2018. The dedication of a contemporary Shona Bible translation was attended by more than 3,000 church and government leaders in Zimbabwe.

ABOUT THIS EDITION

The Original Shona Union Bible of 1949, titled "Baiberi Magwaro Matȿene aMŋari," is the first complete Bible in the unified Shona language. It was published by the British and Foreign Bible Society using the orthography developed by South African linguist Professor Clement Martyn Doke in his 1931 "Report on the Unification of the Shona Dialects," commissioned by the Government of Southern Rhodesia and the Carnegie Corporation. The Doke orthography employed distinctive characters including ɓ, ɗ, ŋ, ȿ, ʋ, and ɀ, which were later replaced by Latin-letter digraphs such as sv and zv when the Standard Orthography was adopted in 1955. Bibles printed in the Doke characters therefore represent a closed historical window.

Jesus teaches from a boat off the shore of Lake Gennesaret. He speaks in parables, giving the example of a Pharisee and tax collector going to the temple to pray. As violence fills the earth, God grieves and resolves to begin again. Noah finds favor and builds the ark. The flood comes and recedes, and God establishes His covenant with Noah, setting the rainbow in the sky as a sign for every generation.

Chapter 4

The Lord's Covenant with Abraham

Chapter 4

Genesis 12, 15, 17

The Lord's Covenant with Abraham

God calls Abram out of his homeland and promises to make him a great nation through whom all peoples will be blessed. In a vision and through the sign of circumcision, God formalizes His covenant with Abraham and his descendants.

Chapter 5

The Birth of Isaac

Chapter 5

Genesis 18, 21

The Birth of Isaac

Long after Abraham and Sarah have given up hope of children, the Lord visits them and reaffirms His promise. Sarah laughs, but in the appointed time Isaac — the child of promise — is born.

Chapter 6

Abraham Tested

Chapter 6

Genesis 22

Abraham Tested

God tests Abraham's faith by commanding him to offer his only son Isaac on Mount Moriah. As Abraham raises the knife, the Lord intervenes, providing a ram in Isaac's place — a defining picture of trust, sacrifice, and God's provision.

Chapter 7

Joseph's Dream

Chapter 7

Genesis 37

Joseph's Dream

Jacob's favored son Joseph dreams that his family will one day bow before him. His brothers' jealousy boils over, and they sell him into slavery in Egypt — beginning a long providential journey that will preserve the family of promise.

Chapter 8

Joseph and Potiphar's Wife

Chapter 8

Genesis 39

Joseph and Potiphar's Wife

In Egypt, Joseph rises to a place of trust in the household of Potiphar. Falsely accused by Potiphar's wife after refusing her advances, he is thrown into prison — yet the Lord remains with him.

Chapter 9

Joseph's Brothers Go to Egypt

Chapter 9

Genesis 41–45

Joseph's Brothers Go to Egypt

Years later, Joseph has risen to become governor of Egypt. When famine drives his brothers down from Canaan in search of grain, they unknowingly come before the brother they betrayed. Joseph reveals himself, forgives them, and the family of Israel is reunited and resettled in Egypt.

Chapter 10

The Israelites Oppressed

Chapter 10

Exodus 1–2

The Israelites Oppressed

Generations later a new pharaoh arises who does not remember Joseph. The Hebrews multiply and are forced into bitter slavery. Among them a Hebrew boy named Moses is hidden in the reeds and grows up in Pharaoh's own household.

Chapter 11

Moses and the Burning Bush

Chapter 11

Exodus 3–4

Moses and the Burning Bush

After fleeing Egypt, Moses keeps flocks in Midian. On Mount Horeb the Lord appears in a bush that burns without being consumed and commissions Moses to return to Egypt and bring His people out of slavery.

Chapter 12

The Passover, the Exodus, and the Covenant at Sinai

Chapter 12

Exodus 5–20 and beyond

The Passover, the Exodus, and the Covenant at Sinai

Moses confronts Pharaoh, the plagues fall on Egypt, and the Passover lamb is slain. Israel is freed and crosses the Red Sea on dry ground. In the wilderness God provides manna and quail, gives the Ten Commandments at Sinai, and renews His covenant with His people — calling them to choose life and the promised land that lies ahead.

his 1995 Shona Genesis portion was issued by the Bible Society of Zimbabwe, the national agency of the United Bible Societies, for a language with some fourteen million speakers across Zimbabwe and parts of Mozambique and Zambia. Shona, called chiShona by its own speakers, is a central Bantu language (Guthrie S.10) encompassing the Zezuru, Karanga, Manyika, Korekore, and Ndau dialect groups.

The first Shona translation work was the Karanga Gospel of Mark of 1905, produced by the Dutch Reformed mission at Morgenster in Masvingo, and the London Missionary Society and Methodist missions followed with portions in Zezuru and Manyika. A Union Shona Bible, based on a compromise Zezuru-Karanga-Manyika orthography agreed at a 1931 conference under the linguist Clement Doke, was published in 1949. Subsequent revisions produced the 1966 Shona Bible and the 1981 Bhaibheri Dzvene, both Bible Society editions.

The 1995 Genesis portion accompanies the modern Shona translation programme centred in Harare. It uses the orthography standardised by the Doke conference and the subsequent Unified Shona of 1955, with the five-vowel inventory and the characteristic whistled sibilants sv and zv. The paperbound portion was distributed for teaching and congregational use through the Bible Society's Harare and Bulawayo offices and by denominational partners.

his Shona Gospel of John was issued by the Bible Society of Zimbabwe for the Shona-speaking population of Zimbabwe and adjacent Mozambique. Shona (ISO 639-3 sna) is a Bantu macrolanguage covering the Karanga, Zezuru, Manyika, Korekore, and Ndau dialect clusters, with around 10 million speakers across Zimbabwe's central plateau and the Manica and Sofala provinces of Mozambique (Ethnologue: sna).

Shona scripture has a tangled history of competing dialect-based translations in the early twentieth century, when Methodist, Anglican, and Roman Catholic missions each produced portions in their own regional varieties (Chikaranga, Chizezuru, Chimanyika). Clement Doke's 1931 orthographic reform established "Standard Shona," a literary form drawing primarily on Zezuru and Karanga, which became the basis for the Shona Bible (Bhaibheri) published in stages by the British and Foreign Bible Society through the mid-twentieth century. A major revision, the Bhaibheri Dzvene muChiShona Chanhasi, was issued in 2005 in contemporary Shona orthography.

The Gospel of John booklet circulates as a stand-alone evangelistic portion from the Bible Society of Zimbabwe catalogue, available in either the older Bhaibheri in Ndimi Dzinonzwika (Union Shona) or the 2005 contemporary revision. It is used across the Anglican, Methodist, Reformed, Roman Catholic, and Apostolic Faith Mission congregations, as well as the indigenous African Initiated Churches that dominate the Shona religious landscape.

his Shona New Testament is a Bible Society of Zimbabwe printing in Shona (ISO 639-3 sna), a Bantu language of the Niger-Congo family spoken by about fourteen million people in Zimbabwe and in adjacent parts of Mozambique, Botswana, and South Africa. Shona is a cluster of closely related dialects, principally Karanga, Zezuru, Korekore, Manyika, and Ndau, unified as a single literary language through the twentieth century.

Early Scripture work was carried out by Dutch Reformed missionaries in Masvingo (then Fort Victoria) and by Jesuits in the Zambezia mission, producing dialect-specific portions through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Clement Doke, the South African linguist, carried out the standardisation study that produced the Shona Unified orthography of 1931, which became the basis of the cross-dialect written language. A Shona Unified New Testament was issued in 1941 and a complete Bible in 1949, with Andries Louw of the Dutch Reformed Church as principal translator.

The printed Shona New Testament in this collection is a Bible Society of Zimbabwe twentieth-century edition in the Unified orthography, continuing the Louw translation line with revisions. A separate common-language Shona Bible (Bhaibheri Idzva) appeared in the 1990s. Distribution is across the Zimbabwean Protestant and Catholic churches, with separate Manyika, Ndau, and Korekore editions also in use among the Anglican dioceses of Mashonaland and the Catholic dioceses of Mutare and Chinhoyi.
